title: What’s happened to the global rules-based order?
gist: Grenville argues the 'rules-based order' is not a hegemon-dependent Bretton Woods edifice but a self-enforcing web of mutually beneficial agreements, so globalisation will route around Trump's tariffs (trade rose from 15% to ~60% of GDP even as Bretton Woods institutions atrophied). The real damage is in non-self-interested domains — aid, refugees, climate — and Trump's novel use of tariffs as a primary coercive security tool; Australia should stay open to all and keep trading with China.

themes.theme: Two views of the rules-based order

insights.claim: Security-focused analysts treat the rules-based order as fixed 'stone tablets' for which Trump's trade assault is a game-changer, while economists see it as an amorphous accumulation of agreements that will adapt to minimise damage.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Economist framing implies markets may be over-pricing fragmentation risk from tariffs.

insights.claim: World trade as a share of GDP rose from 15% in 1950 to almost 60% in 2024, and international investment grew from almost nothing after the Second World War to around 5% of GDP in 2007.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Long-run globalisation baseline against which current tariff shocks should be measured.
insights.quote: world trade (imports and exports) as a percent of GDP – rose from 15% in 1950 to almost 60% in 2024

insights.claim: Globalisation grew even as Bretton Woods institutions atrophied: fixed exchange rates only took practical effect in the late 1950s and broke down within a decade, ending with Nixon's 1971 suspension of gold convertibility, and GATT tariff rounds ran out of steam before the failed 2001 Doha Round.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Hegemonic decline need not imply de-globalisation; the enabling environment is broader than US-led institutions.
insights.quote: Globalisation grew even as the Bretton Woods institutions atrophied.

insights.claim: Much of the rules architecture — on marine trade, aviation, communications, IP, sanitary standards, space and pollution — predates Bretton Woods and persists because each party gains; rules survive only via negotiation ensuring mutual gains.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Technical/plumbing agreements are robust; bet on continuity of trade infrastructure even amid tariff politics.

insights.claim: Trade is intrinsically win-win rather than the zero-sum contest Trump envisages, and retaliating against tariffs is 'like putting rocks in your own harbour'.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Implies retaliation by trading partners is self-harming; expect limited tit-for-tat from rational middle powers.
insights.quote: like putting rocks in your own harbour

insights.claim: The public has never been convinced of free trade — illustrated by the 1999 Seattle WTO protests — and in America the Democrats are also dubious about free trade.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Protectionism is bipartisan in the US; don't expect tariff reversal under a Democratic administration.
insights.quote: In America, the Democrats are dubious about free trade.

insights.claim: Countries have never honoured the GATT/WTO most-favoured-nation principle: the European Union discriminates against outsiders and protects agriculture, and so-called free-trade agreements are actually preferential discriminatory arrangements.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: The 'pre-Trump order' was less rule-bound than nostalgia suggests.

insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Tariff risk is now driven by security/political triggers, not trade fundamentals — harder to model.

insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville

themes.theme: Why trade will route around barriers

insights.claim: US attempts to restrict Chinese imports have rerouted trade via intermediaries, confirming that tariffs mainly harm the country imposing them.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Trade-diversion hubs (intermediary economies) benefit from US-China tariffs; watch transshipment enforcement.
insights.quote: Trade finds a way around barriers, like flowing water.
insights.locator: Trade finds a way around barriers

insights.claim: Trump is a mercantilist disliking imports and current account deficits but does not favour autarky and welcomes foreign investment.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Inbound FDI into the US remains welcome even as imports are penalised — supports onshoring capex plays.
insights.quote: Trump is a mercantilist, disliking imports and current account deficits.
insights.locator: Trade finds a way around barriers

insights.claim: China seeks the option of self-sufficiency but still imports nearly 20% of GDP, high for such a large economy.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: China remains structurally import-dependent — a lever for exporters like Australia.
insights.quote: still has high imports (nearly 20% of GDP)

insights.claim: History suggests sanctions and financial restrictions have only temporary impact as workarounds evolve, and the enormous economic penalty of splitting into self-sufficient blocs argues against full fragmentation.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Fade extreme bloc-fragmentation scenarios; sanctions effects decay over time.

insights.claim: Australia will not stop trading with China, whatever America threatens.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Australia-China trade flows (iron ore, LNG etc.) remain resilient to US pressure.
insights.quote: Australia will not stop trading with China, whatever America threatens.

insights.claim: Market-based exchange rates appear to work satisfactorily with little intervention, and many agreements do not need universal participation since smaller like-minded groups can find useful alignment.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Plurilateral deals are the main channel for new trade rules.

insights.claim: Non-self-interested international efforts — aid, humanitarian programs and refugee programs — have been weakened, and collective-action problems like climate change need a coordinating hegemon, making Trump's departure from the Paris Accord a serious blow.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Climate coordination and aid flows are the most exposed areas — negative for multilateral climate finance.
insights.quote: Trump’s departure from the Paris Accord is a serious blow

insights.claim: Issues like seabed mining, which pit environmental arguments against commercial advantage, may be resolved by power rather than rational analysis.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Deep-sea mining governance likely to be shaped unilaterally by powerful states.

insights.claim: Australia's best policy is to maintain openness, avoid special exclusive trade relationships and remain open to investment from all, with the WTO's non-discrimination principle still good guidance.
insights.speaker: Stephen Grenville
insights.so_what: Argues against Australia joining exclusive US-aligned trade blocs at China's expense.
